skill.displayName: Pet Adaptive Drying Temperature Recommendation | 宠物烘干温度自适应推荐

version.changelog:
- Updated version and minor metadata in SKILL.md.
- Removed the skill-card.md file.
- No functional or workflow changes; documentation only.

llm.summary: The skill is a real pet-media analysis wrapper, but it silently creates or reuses user identities, persists authentication tokens, and can query cloud history with broad automatic triggers.

dimensions.detail: The skill reads local media files, forwards supplied URLs to a remote service, reads OpenClaw/Feishu identity environment variables, and checks a workspace data key file. Remote processing is expected, but private URL and ambient identity handling are not tightly scoped.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: No install-time execution or remote payload retrieval was found; the package ships Python scripts, bundled shared libraries, and declared dependencies. The bundled common library contains the sensitive identity and token behavior.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill tells the agent to auto-trigger on uploaded pet media and broad history-report keywords, and it explicitly instructs the agent not to ask for or reveal internal identity values, reducing user-visible control over account-scoped operations.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The common utility creates a workspace data directory and SQLite database, creates or reuses a default user, and stores access/open tokens for future runs; this persistence is only partially disclosed and lacks clear user opt-in or cleanup guidance.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: Cloud pet image/video analysis is consistent with the stated purpose, but the implementation also performs silent identity provisioning, account login/registration, token persistence, and cloud history retrieval that exceed a simple drying-temperature recommendation flow.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Review this skill before installing. It will send pet media or supplied URLs to lifeemergence.com services, may create or reuse an internal account identifier, can store authentication tokens in the workspace data directory, and can query cloud-stored history when report-history keywords are used. Install only if you are comfortable with that account linkage and remote processing behavior.
llm.findings:
[TP4] unexpected: Artifact evidence supports the core concern: OpenIdUtil reads workspace identity material or creates a default user, while RequestUtil silently calls a phoneLogin/register endpoint and stores returned tokens. This is not enough for a malicious verdict, but it is a material Review concern.
[SDI-1] unexpected: The identity and token database behavior is real and durable. Cloud history access can justify some identity use, but the account lifecycle and reusable token storage are under-scoped for the advertised pet drying recommendation skill.
[SQP-2] expected: The manifest discloses server-side APIs for uploads and URLs, so remote processing itself is expected. The remaining issue is consent clarity for local files, backend-fetched URLs, history retrieval, and retention/account linkage.
[SQP-1] unexpected: The default media trigger and automatic history-report trigger are broad for a skill that can transmit files/URLs and query account-scoped cloud records; explicit confirmation would better match the sensitivity.
[LP3] unexpected: The artifact does not define a narrow permission boundary for filesystem, network, environment, or persistence access. Those capabilities are partly necessary, but their scope is broader than the user-facing task explains.
[YR4] expected: Manual review did not find hidden control characters or prompt-injection content in the manifest; the YARA-style metadata signal appears to be explainable by long bilingual metadata and formatting, so it was downgraded.
[P9] expected: The whitespace-padding report points to normal Python line wrapping/alignment in the inspected file, not concealed instructions; it did not affect the verdict.
